comments.body:
Fix implemented (RED->GREEN, held-out oracle).

Root cause confirmed as filed: hostname is not host identity inside a container.
Verified empirically with real containers on this host — two `docker run` recreates:
  host=4f2e3e889406 boot=43582fc9-e87a-4870-8ddd-f0b980324696 ns=33058232
  host=3790c7a6034a boot=43582fc9-e87a-4870-8ddd-f0b980324696 ns=33059117
The hostname re-rolls per recreate (the bug's trigger); the kernel boot id is IDENTICAL
(so it is a sound same-host identity); the pid-namespace inode DIFFERS (so the stamped pid
is genuinely not probeable across the recreate — a pid probe alone cannot fix this).

Fix (src/rebar/_store/lock.py only):
- v2 owner stamp `rebar-lock v2 host=<hostid> ns=<pidns> pid=<pid> start=<starttime>`,
  where hostid is `boot-<boot_id>` (falling back to `name-<hostname>` off Linux). The stamp
  is colon-free, so an older rebar's `partition(":")` parse finds no separator and declines
  to act — forward-safe.
- `_mkdir_lock_is_stale(lock_dir, *, fcntl_held=False)`: a different host identity is still
  never reclaimed (yaw-gravel-linen intact, unconditionally); a same-host owner in the SAME
  pid namespace is still judged by probing the pid, now start-time qualified so a recycled
  pid cannot masquerade as the owner; a same-host owner in a DIFFERENT pid namespace (the
  container recreate) is reclaimed only under the fcntl proof.
- The fcntl proof: `_acquire_mkdir` is only reached while `acquire()` already holds the
  exclusive `fcntl.flock` leg on the same tracker, held for the whole lifetime of the mkdir
  leg. flock is kernel-mediated on the inode, shared across pid/mount namespaces on ONE
  kernel and released when its holder dies; a v2 stamp is only written by an acquirer that
  took the fcntl leg first. Same boot id + we hold that lock ⇒ positive proof the owner is
  gone. This is a STRONGER proof than the pid probe it stands in for, not a loosening — and
  it deliberately does not extend across boot ids.

Deliberately NOT added: an age ceiling that reclaims unprovable foreign-host locks. That is
the exact "loosen the guard" move yaw-gravel-linen forbids. AC3 is met instead by making the
incident class provable (no stall at all) — run_ensures already logs a WARNING on LockTimeout
rather than swallowing it silently. The remaining stall-on-boot budget concern is filed
separately rather than widening this fix's scope.

Evidence: 7 new tests in tests/unit/test_lock_container_recreate.py, held out from the
implementer. All 7 RED first; the mechanism-level RED against unfixed code reproduced the
incident exactly (LockTimeout on a same-host, dead-pid, changed-container-id orphan). Four
defect-seeded mutations each returned the oracle to RED: (1) hostname as host identity ->
the original LockTimeout, (2) foreign-host guard removed, (3) fcntl proof no longer required,
(4) start-time qualification removed. End-to-end replication through the real entry point
(rebar.comment past the orphan): 0.18s, vs the incident's ~62s-then-fail.

compiled_state.description:
## Context / Problem

An orphaned store write-lock froze the review-bot's startup on the Gerrit host for over an hour on
2026-07-31, causing seven consecutive autodeploy failures (CloudWatch alarm `rebar-autodeploy-errors`,
18:21 UTC onward). The lock could never be reclaimed, by design, and would not have self-healed.

`src/rebar/_store/lock.py`:
- `_owner_stamp()` (:152-154) writes `f"{socket.gethostname()}:{os.getpid()}"` into the lock dir.
- `_mkdir_lock_is_stale()` (:171-190) returns `False` unless `host == socket.gethostname()` (:184).

Inside a container `socket.gethostname()` is the **container id**, and docker assigns a NEW one on
every `compose up -d` recreate. So a lock orphaned by the SAME host's previous container is
classified as a **foreign-host** lock — the shared-filesystem case the guard was written for — and is
never reclaimed. There is no age-based ceiling, so the orphan is permanent.

The conservatism itself is deliberate and correct in its intended setting; the docstring says "never
reclaim on anything short of proof (bug yaw-gravel-linen)". The defect is that **hostname is not host
identity inside a container**, so the foreign-host branch misfires for what is actually the same host.

## Observed (production, 2026-07-31)

- Lock dir `/var/gerrit/site/reviewbot-tickets/.ticket-write.lock.d/`, created 18:30:49, owner stamp
  `1e0fab75d5bd:3085`. Container `1e0fab75d5bd` ran 18:03:46-18:30:55 and was SIGKILLed mid-store-write
  when a deploy recreated it (it logged a completed code_review artifact link and `Shutting down` in
  the same second).
- Every later container has a different id, so `_mkdir_lock_is_stale` returned False forever.
- `run_ensures()` (`_store/ensures.py:158`) calls `write_lock()` with the defaults
  `_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=30` x `_DEFAULT_ATTEMPTS=2` = a 60s budget, then swallows `LockTimeout`. Startup
  therefore took ~62s instead of <4s, exceeding autodeploy's `HEALTH_TIMEOUT=30`, so every deploy was
  rolled back to `:prev`.
- Journal evidence (spans 2026-07-03 -> 2026-07-31): 197 `is a writable rebar store` lines vs 183
  `ensure env-id` lines = 14 lock-timeout boots, ALL on 2026-07-31 from 18:30:49 onward, zero in the
  preceding four weeks. `.ensure-applied` remained stamped at the last successful sweep, 18:03.
- Cleared manually by removing the orphaned lock dir; this ticket is the durable fix.

## Approach

Make the owner stamp stable across container recreates on one host (e.g. boot_id + pid, or a
start-time-qualified pid) so a same-host orphan is provably reclaimable, and/or add an age-based
reclaim ceiling so a lock that cannot be proven live is reclaimable after a bounded interval. Keep
the existing refusal-without-proof behaviour for the genuine shared-filesystem case.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/_store/lock.py` — `_owner_stamp`, `_mkdir_lock_is_stale`, `_reclaim_mkdir_lock`.
- Tests for the container-recreate scenario and the shared-filesystem scenario.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A lock orphaned by a dead process on the SAME host is reclaimable even when the recorded
      hostname differs because the process ran in a since-recreated container; verified by a test that
      simulates a changed `gethostname()` with a dead pid.
- [ ] A lock owned by a LIVE process is still never reclaimed, and a genuinely foreign-host lock is
      still not reclaimed on the strength of hostname alone; verified by tests (no regression of
      bug yaw-gravel-linen).
- [ ] An unprovable lock does not block indefinitely: either an age ceiling applies or the failure is
      surfaced rather than silently swallowed into a 60s stall.
- [ ] make lint, make typecheck, and the default suite exit zero.
compiled_state.title: Store mkdir lock is permanently unreclaimable inside a container: gethostname() is the container id, so a same-host orphan looks foreign-host
